lesson.child_mission: Good research questions are open enough to need investigation but clear enough to answer with facts; closed yes/no questions are often too thin.

lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Rewrite "Do shadows exist?" as a stronger research question.

FEEDBACK
Example: Why do shadows change length during the day?

CHECK
Questions that already contain the full answer are not research questions.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Write ten research questions on two topics. Label each open or closed. Keep your three strongest open questions and justify why they are researchable.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Good research questions are open enough to need investigation but clear enough to answer with facts; closed yes/no questions are often too thin.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.
lesson.parent_notes:
Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: Write ten research questions on two topics. Label each open or closed. Keep your three strongest open questions and justify why they are researchable. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using question on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Written model 2: Sample error: Questions that already contain the full answer are not research questions.. Correction: Example: Why do shadows change length during the day?. Why it helps the audience is stated.

Parent: Likely misconception: Questions that already contain the full answer are not research questions. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating question on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with question, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about question with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for question. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
Thin: "Are bees cool?" Stronger: "How do honeybees communicate the direction of flowers?"

TRY FIRST
Rewrite "Do shadows exist?" as a stronger research question.

FEEDBACK
Example: Why do shadows change length during the day?
teach_steps.explain:
Good research questions are open enough to need investigation but clear enough to answer with facts; closed yes/no questions are often too thin.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
teach_steps.notice: Questions that already contain the full answer are not research questions. Correct the meaning, not just the appearance.
